args.CodeContent:
# Walkthrough — Backend Documentation & OpenAPI / Swagger Integration

## 1. Overview of Accomplishments

In accordance with [`agents/rules/MD_CONVENTION.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/agents/rules/MD_CONVENTION.md) and [`agents/rules/COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/agents/rules/COMMIT_CONVENTION.md), we have fully documented the Scientific RAG Backend architecture, created API specifications, and integrated interactive **OpenAPI 3.0 / Swagger UI** for all endpoints.

---

## 2. Documentation Governance & Authoritative Reports

### 2.1 Governance Standards Established
- [`agents/rules/MD_CONVENTION.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/agents/rules/MD_CONVENTION.md):
  - Mandatory 7-field header (`Motivation/Background`, `Purpose`, `Overview Pipeline`, `Detailed Plan`, `References`, `Created`, `Last Updated`).
  - Strict ISO 8601 timestamps (`2026-10-14T17:05:00+07:00`).
  - Active clickable cross-reference links (`file:///...`).
  - Lifecycle state tracking (`[STATUS: COMPLETED]`).
- [`agents/rules/COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/agents/rules/COMMIT_CONVENTION.md):
  - Conventional Commits specification.
  - Documented-Commit mandate with `Companion-Doc:` Git trailers for machine parseability.

### 2.2 Authoritative Engineering Documents
1. [`docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md):
   - Mermaid sequence diagram depicting request flow through controller, embedding service, LanceDB (913,205 vectors), graph reranker, and local Qwen2.5-7B on GPU.
   - Cross-platform GPU acceleration details (CUDA on RTX 4060 with 99 layers offloaded; Apple Silicon Metal/MPS).
   - Co-authorship PageRank ($0.15$) and association rules query expansion math.
   - Strict citation grounding rules (`[Paper: {paper_id}]`).
2. [`docs/API_SPECIFICATION.md`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/docs/API_SPECIFICATION.md):
   - Formal specification of all request/response schemas, DTOs, parameters, and error codes.

---

## 3. OpenAPI & Swagger UI Integration

### 3.1 Packages Installed in `backend_rag`
- `@nestjs/swagger` (`^11.0.0`)
- `swagger-ui-express` (`^5.0.0`)

### 3.2 Annotated Components
- **[`backend_rag/src/rag/dto/query.dto.ts`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/backend_rag/src/rag/dto/query.dto.ts)**:
  - Decorated with `@ApiProperty` and `@ApiPropertyOptional` including field constraints, defaults, and realistic examples.
- **[`backend_rag/src/rag/dto/response.dto.ts`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/backend_rag/src/rag/dto/response.dto.ts)**:
  - Typed Swagger DTOs: `GroundedChunkDto`, `RAGSynthesisResponseDto`, `GpuStatusDto`, `HealthComponentsDto`, and `HealthResponseDto`.
- **[`backend_rag/src/rag/rag.controller.ts`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/backend_rag/src/rag/rag.controller.ts)**:
  - Tagged under `@ApiTags('Scientific RAG')`.
  - Operations documented: `POST /api/rag/chat` and `GET /api/rag/health`.
- **[`backend_rag/src/main.ts`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/backend_rag/src/main.ts)**:
  - Swagger setup mounted at `/api/docs` (interactive UI) and `/api/docs-json` (raw OpenAPI 3.0 JSON).

---

## 4. Verification Results

### 4.1 Automated Validation
- `npx tsc --noEmit` -> Passed with 0 errors.
- `npm test` -> All 6 test suites passed (16 tests passed).
- `npm run build` -> Clean NestJS 11 build into `dist/`.

### 4.2 Live Swagger UI & Schema Verification
- **Swagger UI**: Accessible at `http://localhost:8000/api/docs` (Returns HTTP 200, `text/html`).
- **OpenAPI 3.0 Schema**: Accessible at `http://localhost:8000/api/docs-json`:
  ```json
  {
    "openapi": "3.0.0",
    "info": {
      "title": "Scientific Literature RAG API",
      "version": "1.0.0"
    },
    "paths": {
      "/api/rag/chat": { ... },
      "/api/rag/health": { ... }
    },
    "components": {

1: # Scientific Literature RAG System (TypeScript)
2: 
3: [![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5.7-3178C6?style=flat&logo=typescript&logoColor=white)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/)
4: [![NestJS](https://img.shields.io/badge/NestJS-11.0-E0234E?style=flat&logo=nestjs&logoColor=white)](https://nestjs.com/)
5: [![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-16.4-black?style=flat&logo=next.js&logoColor=white)](https://nextjs.org/)
6: [![LanceDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/LanceDB-0.40-black?style=flat)](https://lancedb.com/)
7: [![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind_CSS-4.0-38B2AC?style=flat&logo=tailwind-css&logoColor=white)](https://tailwindcss.com/)
8: 
9: An end-to-end, high-performance Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform implemented entirely in **TypeScript / Node.js**. The system is built over a Medallion Lakehouse comprising **13,000+ scientific research papers** and **164,800+ dense 768-dimensional embeddings** across AI, Machine Learning, Computer Vision, and NLP.
10: 
11: ---
12: 
13: ## 🏛️ System Architecture
14: 
15: ```mermaid
16: flowchart TD
17:     subgraph DATA_TIER["Medallion Lakehouse & Model Assets"]
18:         GoldLance[("LanceDB Vector Store\n(164k+ 768-D Chunks)")]
19:         GoldMining[("Mining Artifacts\n• PageRank Graph\n• FP-Growth Rules")]
20:         ModelStore[("Local LLM Weights\nQwen2.5-7B GGUF")]
21:     end
22: 
23:     subgraph BACKEND["Backend Service (backend_rag: NestJS)"]
24:         Embedder["Embedding Engine\n(Nomic v1.5 with 'search_query:')"]
25:         Retriever["LanceDB Vector Retriever\n(Cosine Similarity)"]
26:         Reranker["Authority Reranker\n(PageRank Boost + Rule Expansion)"]
27:         LLMInference["LLM Runner & Grounding Engine\n(node-llama-cpp)"]
28:         RagController["REST API (/api/rag/chat)"]
29: 
30:         RagController --> Embedder --> Retriever --> Reranker --> LLMInference --> RagController
31:     end
32: 
33:     subgraph FRONTEND["Frontend Client (frontend_rag: Next.js 16)"]
34:         ChatUI["Interactive Research Chat"]
35:         CitationView["Citation & Provenance Inspector"]
36:         PaperPreview["Full Paper & Metadata Viewer"]
37: 
38:         ChatUI <--> CitationView
39:     end
40: 
41:     GoldLance <--> Retriever
42:     GoldMining <--> Reranker
43:     ModelStore <--> LLMInference
44:     FRONTEND <-->|"HTTP / SSE JSON"| RagController
45: ```
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 📦 Repository Organization
50: 
51: | Directory / Package | Description | Technology Stack |
52: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
53: | **[`backend_rag/`](file:///Users/quangmanh/Project/RAG_TS/backend_rag)** | Backend RAG service providing vector retrieval, mining-based reranking, and local LLM generation. | NestJS 11, `@lancedb/lancedb`, `@xenova/transformers`, `node-llama-cpp` |
54: | **[`frontend_rag/`](file:///Users/quangmanh/Project/RAG_TS/frontend_rag)** | Modern web client for querying the RAG pipeline and exploring cited papers. | Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, TypeScript |
55: | **[`docs/`](file:///Users/quangmanh/Project/RAG_TS/docs)** | Comprehensive architectural documentation, data schemas, and prompt specifications. | Markdown, Mermaid |
56: | **[`data/`](file:///Users/quangmanh/Project/RAG_TS/data)** | Symlink/Directory to Medallion lakehouse tiers (`raw/`, `silver/`, `gold/`). | LanceDB, Parquet, JSON |
57: | **[`model/`](file:///Users/quangmanh/Project/RAG_TS/model)** | Local quantized LLM weights (`qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf`). | GGUF |
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 📚 Key Technical Highlights
62: 
63: 1. **Strict Asymmetric Query Embedding**: Uses `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5` via `@xenova/transformers`. Enforces prefix `search_query:` on inputs to match pre-indexed document chunk representations.
64: 2. **Dense Vector Search**: Powered by `@lancedb/lancedb` against 164,876 scientific chunks, optimized for sub-second Cosine search.
65: 3. **Graph-Mining Boosted Reranking**: Incorporates PageRank co-authorship authority metrics (`graph_coauthorship.json`) and FP-Growth association rules (`association_rules.json`) to elevate seminal papers and discover co-occurring research topics.
66: 4. **Zero-Hallucination Academic Grounding**: Enforces strict system instructions requiring citations in the format `[Paper: {paper_id}]`. Refuses to answer outside the retrieved context.
67: 5. **Local Hardware Acceleration**: Runs local LLMs with Metal (Apple Silicon) or CUDA GPU offloading via `node-llama-cpp`.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## ⚡ Quick Start
72: 
73: ### 1. Prerequisites
74: - **Node.js**: v20+ (Node.js 22 LTS recommended)
75: - **C++ Compiler & CMake**: Required for native bindings in `node-llama-cpp`
76: - **Model File**: GGUF model located in `model/` (e.g., `qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf`)
77: - **Data Lakehouse**: Gold LanceDB store located in `data/gold/lancedb`
78: 
79: ### 2. Setup & Run Backend
80: 
81: ```bash
82: cd backend_rag
83: cp .env_example .env
84: npm install
85: npm run start:dev
86: ```
87: > The backend server starts at `http://localhost:3001`.
88: 
89: ### 3. Setup & Run Frontend

93: npm install
94: npm run dev
95: ```
96: > The frontend application starts at `http://localhost:3000`.

args.CodeContent:
# Scientific Literature RAG System (TypeScript)

[![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-5.7-3178C6?style=flat&logo=typescript&logoColor=white)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/)
[![NestJS](https://img.shields.io/badge/NestJS-11.0-E0234E?style=flat&logo=nestjs&logoColor=white)](https://nestjs.com/)
[![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-16.4-black?style=flat&logo=next.js&logoColor=white)](https://nextjs.org/)
[![LanceDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/LanceDB-0.40-black?style=flat)](https://lancedb.com/)
[![OpenAPI / Swagger](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swagger-OpenAPI_3.0-85EA2D?style=flat&logo=swagger&logoColor=black)](http://localhost:8000/api/docs)
[![CUDA](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardware-NVIDIA_CUDA_%26_Metal-76B900?style=flat&logo=nvidia&logoColor=white)](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit)

An end-to-end, high-performance Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform implemented in **TypeScript / NestJS 11**. The system is built over an optimized Medallion Lakehouse comprising **913,205 dense 768-dimensional embeddings** across AI, Machine Learning, Computer Vision, and NLP, accelerated locally via **`node-llama-cpp`** on GPU.

---

## 🏛️ System Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph DATA_TIER["Medallion Lakehouse & Model Assets"]
        GoldLance[("LanceDB Vector Store\n(913,205 768-D Chunks\nCompacted 10 Blocks)")]
        GoldMining[("Mining Artifacts\n• PageRank Graph (40 Influencers)\n• FP-Growth Association Rules")]
        ModelStore[("Local LLM Weights\nQwen2.5-7B Instruct GGUF\n(4.68 GB)")]
    end

    subgraph BACKEND["Backend Service (backend_rag: NestJS 11)"]
        Swagger["OpenAPI 3.0 / Swagger UI\n(/api/docs & /api/docs-json)"]
        Embedder["Embedding Engine\n(Nomic v1.5 with 'search_query:')"]
        Retriever["LanceDB Vector Retriever\n(Cosine Distance ANN)"]
        Reranker["Graph Hybrid Reranker\n(0.85 Sim + 0.15 PageRank Authority)"]
        GpuDetector["Hardware Profiler\n(NVIDIA CUDA / Apple Metal)"]
        LLMInference["LLM Runner & Grounding Engine\n(node-llama-cpp, 99 GPU Layers)"]
        RagController["REST API (/api/rag/chat & /api/rag/health)"]

        RagController --> Embedder --> Retriever --> Reranker --> LLMInference --> RagController
        Swagger -.-> RagController
        GpuDetector -.-> LLMInference
    end

    subgraph FRONTEND["Frontend Client (frontend_rag: Next.js 16)"]
        ChatUI["Interactive Research Chat"]
        CitationView["Citation & Provenance Inspector"]
        PaperPreview["Full Paper & Metadata Viewer"]

        ChatUI <--> CitationView
    end

    GoldLance <--> Retriever
    GoldMining <--> Reranker
    ModelStore <--> LLMInference
    FRONTEND <-->|"HTTP JSON"| RagController
```

---

## 📦 Repository Organization

| Directory / Package | Description | Technology Stack |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **[`backend_rag/`](backend_rag/)** | Backend RAG service providing vector retrieval, mining-based reranking, local GPU LLM generation, and Swagger UI. | NestJS 11, `@lancedb/lancedb`, `@xenova/transformers`, `node-llama-cpp`, `@nestjs/swagger` |
| **[`frontend_rag/`](frontend_rag/)** | Modern web client for querying the RAG pipeline and exploring cited papers. | Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, TypeScript |
| **[`docs/`](docs/)** | Comprehensive architectural documentation, API specifications, and prompt contracts. | Markdown, Mermaid (`MD_CONVENTION.md`, `COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`) |
| **[`agents/rules/`](agents/rules/)** | Immutable documentation and commit standards (`MD_CONVENTION.md`, `COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`). | Markdown standard specifications |
| **[`data/`](data/)** | Local lakehouse junction / Cloudflare R2 bucket connection (`gold/lancedb`, `gold/mining`). | LanceDB, Parquet, JSON |
| **[`models/`](models/)** | Local quantized LLM weights (`qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf`). | GGUF |

---

## 📚 Key Technical Highlights

1. **Hardware Acceleration (NVIDIA CUDA & Apple Metal)**:
   - Built-in automatic GPU detection via [`gpu.util.ts`](backend_rag/src/utils/gpu.util.ts) supporting Windows/Linux CUDA (`nvidia-smi`) and macOS Metal (`arm64`).
   - Live hardware tested with **99 GPU layers offloaded** to NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (8,188 MiB VRAM).
2. **Dense Vector Search (913,205 Chunks)**:
   - Ingested and indexed via `@lancedb/lancedb` in 10 compacted data blocks (7.875 GB lakehouse footprint) with sub-second ANN cosine search.
   - S3-compatible fallback for live Cloudflare R2 object storage.
3. **Strict Asymmetric Query Embedding**:
   - Uses `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5` via `@xenova/transformers`. Enforces `search_query: ` prefixing and L2 unit normalization.
4. **Graph-Mining Boosted Reranking**:
   - Incorporates PageRank co-authorship authority metrics (`graph_coauthorship.json`) and FP-Growth association rules (`association_rules.json`).
   - Blended ranking formula: $S_{\text{final}} = 0.85 \times S_{\text{sim}} + 0.15 \times A_{\text{author}}$.
5. **Zero-Hallucination Academic Grounding**:
   - Enforces strict system instructions requiring citations in the format `[Paper: {paper_id}]`.
   - Automated regex extraction of cited paper IDs returned alongside grounded chunks.
6. **Interactive OpenAPI 3.0 / Swagger UI**:
   - Fully documented interactive UI served at `/api/docs` and machine-parseable schema at `/api/docs-json`.

---

## ⚡ Quick Start

### 1. Prerequisites
- **Node.js**: v20+ (Node.js 22 LTS recommended)
- **C++ Build Tools / CMake**: Required for native bindings in `node-llama-cpp`
- **NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit** (Windows/Linux) or **Apple Silicon** (macOS)
- **Model File**: GGUF model located in `models/qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m/qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (4.68 GB)
- **Data Lakehouse**: Gold LanceDB store located in `data/gold/lancedb/scientific_papers_gold.lance`

### 2. Setup & Run Backend

```bash
cd backend_rag
npm install
npm run build
npm run start:prod
```
> The backend server starts at **`http://localhost:8000`**.

### 3. API Endpoints & Swagger Documentation
- **Interactive Swagger UI**: [http://localhost:8000/api/docs](http://localhost:8000/api/docs)
- **OpenAPI 3.0 Schema**: [http://localhost:8000/api/docs-json](http://localhost:8000/api/docs-json)
- **System & GPU Health**: [http://localhost:8000/api/rag/health](http://localhost:8000/api/rag/health)
- **RAG Chat**: `POST http://localhost:8000/api/rag/chat`

#### Example RAG Request:
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/rag/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "How does LoRA optimize large models?", "top_k": 5}'
```

---

## 📖 In-Depth Documentation

For detailed architecture diagrams, API specifications, and prompt contracts, refer to:
- **[`docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md`](docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md)**: Complete system design, sequence diagrams, and GPU telemetry benchmarks.

- **[`docs/prompt.md`](docs/prompt.md)**: System prompt and structured guidance catalog.

### 1. Latency Impact: Increasing `top_k` from 5 to 10

#### 📊 Empirical Benchmark Results (NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop GPU, CUDA 13.0)

| Benchmark Query | `top_k = 5` Latency | `top_k = 10` Latency | Difference (ms) | Percentage Change |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Query 1**: *"How does LoRA optimize large models?"* | **12,877 ms** | **13,345 ms** | +468 ms | **+3.6%** |
| **Query 2**: *"Key differences between Transformer self-attention & ConvNets?"* | **18,819 ms** | **15,484 ms** | -3,335 ms | **-17.7%** *(Output length variation)* |

---

#### 🔍 Pipeline Stage Decomposition

To understand why the latency difference is so small, consider how time is spent in our pipeline:

1. **Embedding & Vector Search (`nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5` + LanceDB)**:
   - Generating the 768-D query vector: $\approx 120\text{–}180\text{ ms}$.
   - LanceDB Cosine ANN scan over **913,205 vectors**:
     - At `top_k = 5`: retrieves 15 candidates ($k \times 3$) in $\approx 25\text{–}35\text{ ms}$.
     - At `top_k = 10`: retrieves 30 candidates ($k \times 3$) in $\approx 35\text{–}48\text{ ms}$.
     - **Delta: $<15\text{ ms}$ (negligible)**.
2. **PageRank & Association Rules Reranking**:
   - In-memory scoring over 15 vs 30 objects takes $<2\text{ ms}$.
3. **Local LLM Prompt Ingestion (Prefill / TTFT)**:
   - Doubling the chunks from 5 to 10 increases prompt context from $\approx 1,200\text{ tokens}$ to $\approx 2,400\text{ tokens}$.
   - Because all 99 layers are offloaded into GPU VRAM (RTX 4060 with Tensor Cores), prompt prefill throughput is very fast ($\approx 250\text{–}350\text{ tokens/sec}$).
   - Ingestion delta: $\approx \frac{1200\text{ tokens}}{300\text{ tokens/s}} \approx 300\text{–}500\text{ ms}$.
4. **LLM Autoregressive Generation (Decode)**:
   - **Generation dominates 95%+ of total latency** ($\approx 35\text{–}40\text{ tokens/sec}$).
   - The total elapsed time depends far more on the **length of the answer generated** (e.g., 300 tokens $\approx 8\text{–}10\text{s}$, 500 tokens $\approx 14\text{–}17\text{s}$) than on the prompt size.

#### 🎯 Conclusion & Recommendation
- **Estimated Net Latency Increase**: **+3% to +10%** (approximately **+400 ms to +900 ms** on GPU).
- **VRAM Impact**: Context memory increases slightly from $\approx 1.2\text{ GB}$ to $\approx 2.4\text{ GB}$ KV-cache; well within the 8,188 MiB VRAM budget.
- **Answer Quality**: `top_k = 10` provides richer multi-paper coverage and cross-paper synthesis without a significant latency penalty on CUDA/Metal.

args.CodeContent:
# Implementation Plan: Next.js 16 Full-Stack Research Workbench Integration

- **Motivation/Background**: With the NestJS 11 Scientific RAG Backend fully implemented, accelerated on local GPU (RTX 4060 CUDA), and documented via Swagger, we now need to complete the full-stack user experience by integrating the `frontend_rag` application.
- **Purpose**: Transform the Next.js 16 frontend (`frontend_rag`) into a production-grade, side-by-side Scientific Research Workbench that connects to the NestJS backend via Next.js API routes (`/api/rag/chat` & `/api/rag/health`), renders markdown math equations, highlights active `[Paper: {id}]` citations, and allows exploring grounded chunks and paper metadata interactively.
- **Overview Pipeline**: 
  1. Create typed interfaces (`frontend_rag/src/types/rag.ts`) matching backend contracts.
  2. Implement Next.js App Router API proxy routes (`app/api/rag/chat/route.ts` & `app/api/rag/health/route.ts`) forwarding requests to `http://localhost:8000`.
  3. Build modular UI components:
     - `Header`: System health badge (GPU status, vector count, model status).
     - `ChatStream`: Conversational history with markdown math support (`react-markdown`, `remark-math`, `rehype-katex`), citation chips (`[Paper: {id}]`), and query controls (`top_k`, `category`, `use_authority_boost`, `expand_query`).
     - `GroundedInspector`: Collapsible right-hand panel displaying retrieved chunks with cosine similarity, PageRank authority scores, blended final score, section title, and full abstract text.
     - `PaperModal`: Deep-dive modal preview for inspected research papers.
  4. Integrate into `app/page.tsx`, run TypeScript verification, test production build, and commit following `COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`.
- **Detailed Plan**: §1 User Decisions from Grill-Me; §2 Proposed Architecture & Components; §3 Verification Plan.
- **References**: `agents/rules/MD_CONVENTION.md`, `agents/rules/COMMIT_CONVENTION.md`, `docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md`, `docs/API_SPECIFICATION.md`.
- **Created**: 2026-10-14T17:30:00+07:00
- **Last Updated**: 2026-10-14T17:30:00+07:00

---

## User Decisions (Resolved via /grill-me)

1. **Focus Milestone**: Next.js 16 Full-Stack Integration connecting `frontend_rag` to `http://localhost:8000/api/rag/chat`.
2. **Interface Layout**: **Side-by-Side Research Workbench** (Left: Conversational chat stream; Right: Collapsible grounded chunks & cited paper inspection cards).
3. **API Architecture**: **Next.js API Proxy Route** (`/api/rag/chat` forwarding server-to-server to NestJS `:8000`).
4. **Interactive Feature Scope**: **Rich Research Suite** (Markdown math rendering, active citation badge highlighting, `top_k` slider, category filter chips, and latency telemetry).

---

## Proposed Changes

### Component 1: TypeScript Types & API Proxy

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/src/types/rag.ts`
- Port `GroundedChunkResult`, `RAGSynthesisResponse`, `HealthResponse`, and `ChatQueryRequest` to the frontend.

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/app/api/rag/chat/route.ts`
- Next.js server-side route handler accepting POST requests, validating body, forwarding to `process.env.BACKEND_URL || 'http://localhost:8000/api/rag/chat'`, and returning typed JSON.

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/app/api/rag/health/route.ts`
- Next.js server-side route handler polling backend health and GPU telemetry.

---

### Component 2: Modular UI Components

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/components/Navbar.tsx`
- Header with system title, arXiv lakehouse badge (`913,205 Vectors`), local LLM tag (`Qwen2.5-7B Instruct`), GPU status badge (`CUDA RTX 4060` or `Metal`), and link to Swagger docs.

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/components/ChatPanel.tsx`
- Conversational chat area with:
  - Input field with query submission (`Enter` to submit).
  - Quick-start scientific query suggestions (e.g., *"How does LoRA optimize large models?"*, *"What are the key differences between Transformer self-attention and convnets?"*).
  - Control bar: `top_k` slider ($1\text{–}15$), arXiv Category select (`All`, `cs.LG`, `cs.CV`, `cs.CL`, `stat.ML`), PageRank authority boost toggle, and query expansion toggle.
  - Message bubble rendering with LaTeX math equations ($\LaTeX$ support via KaTeX) and clickable interactive citation badges (`[Paper: {paper_id}]`).
  - Latency and citation count telemetry tags on each response.

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/components/GroundedInspector.tsx`
- Collapsible right-hand inspector panel:
  - Lists grounded paper chunks for the selected or most recent query.
  - Highlights paper title, authors, section title, and citation tag.
  - Interactive score breakdown bar: Similarity score ($85\%$) vs Authority score ($15\%$) vs Final blended score.
  - Full chunk content viewer.

#### [NEW] `frontend_rag/components/PaperModal.tsx`
- Dialog modal for clicking any citation tag to view the paper's full context, metadata, and link to arXiv (`https://arxiv.org/abs/{paper_id}`).

#### [MODIFY] `frontend_rag/app/page.tsx`
- Implement root workbench page organizing the Navbar, left ChatPanel, and right GroundedInspector in a responsive 2-column layout.

#### [MODIFY] `frontend_rag/app/globals.css`
- Import KaTeX CSS (`katex/dist/katex.min.css`) for equation rendering and custom scrollbar styles.

---

## Verification Plan

### Automated Tests
1. Frontend type checking and production build:
   ```powershell
   cd frontend_rag; npm run build
   ```
2. Lint check:
   ```powershell
   cd frontend_rag; npm run lint
   ```

### Manual Verification
1. Run backend on `:8000` (`node dist/main.js`).
2. Run frontend on `:3000` (`npm run dev` or `npm start`).
3. Send a test query via the web interface:
   - Verify server proxy successfully hits NestJS.
   - Verify GPU inference completes and streams/renders response with citations.
   - Click citation tag `[Paper: 2106.09685]` and confirm it highlights chunk card in right inspector and opens paper modal.
   - Test `top_k` slider from 3 to 10 and verify grounded chunks count updates accordingly.

### Git Commits
- Commit in `frontend_rag` submodule:
  ```text
  feat(workbench): implement Next.js 16 full-stack scientific research workbench

  Companion-Doc: docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md
  ```
- Commit in root repository:
  ```text
  chore(submodule): update frontend_rag with research workbench integration

  Companion-Doc: docs/SCIENTIFIC_RAG_BACKEND.md
  ```

args.CodeContent:
# Walkthrough — Next.js 16 Full-Stack Research Workbench Integration

## 1. Executive Summary

We have built and verified the complete full-stack integration for the **Scientific Literature RAG System**, connecting the modern **Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4)** frontend workbench to the **NestJS 11** backend.

### Key Highlights:
1. **Next.js 16 API Proxy Architecture**:
   - Implemented server-to-server proxy handlers in `frontend_rag/app/api/rag/chat/route.ts` and `frontend_rag/app/api/rag/health/route.ts`.
   - Eliminates browser CORS configuration complexities while exposing unified endpoints.
2. **Side-by-Side Research Workbench Layout**:
   - **Left Column**: Conversational chat interface with quick-start scientific question pills, LaTeX equation rendering (`remark-math`, `rehype-katex`), interactive citation badges (`[Paper: {paper_id}]`), and pipeline parameter controls (`top_k`, arXiv categories, PageRank boost).
   - **Right Column**: Collapsible grounded chunks inspector visualizing cosine similarity ($85\%$) vs author PageRank authority ($15\%$) score bars, section titles, and source paper chunk texts.
3. **Paper Deep-Dive Inspector Modal**:
   - Clicking any citation badge or chunk card triggers an inspection modal with author metadata, full content, and direct links to arXiv (`https://arxiv.org/abs/{paper_id}`).
4. **Live End-to-End Verification**:
   - Sent test query from `http://localhost:3000/api/rag/chat`.
   - Executed full RAG grounding over **913,205 vectors in LanceDB** and synthesized an answer using **local Qwen2.5-7B on NVIDIA CUDA GPU (RTX 4060)** in **13.2 seconds**.

---

## 2. Full-Stack Dataflow Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User as Researcher
    participant UI as Next.js 16 UI (:3000)
    participant NextAPI as Next.js API Proxy (/api/rag/*)

        NestAPI->>NestAPI: Hybrid Reranking (0.85 Sim + 0.15 PageRank)
    end

    rect rgb(250, 240, 255)
        NestAPI->>LLM: Generate Grounded Answer (99 GPU Layers on CUDA)

LoRA optimizes large models by constraining the updates to the pre-trained weight matrices during adaptation to a low-rank decomposition. Specifically, for a pre-trained weight matrix ( W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} ), the update is represented as a low-rank decomposition ( W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA ), where ( B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} ) and ( A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} ), and the rank ( r \ll \min(d, k) ). During training, the pre-trained weight matrix ( W_0 ) is frozen and does not receive gradient updates, while the matrices ( A ) and ( B ) contain trainable parameters. This approach significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters compared to full fine-tuning, making the model more efficient in terms of both storage and computation.

+/**
+ * Standardizes raw model LaTeX output delimiters so remark-math & rehype-katex
+ * render both inline and block equations reliably.
+ * Specifically converts:
+ *  - \[ ... \] and $$ ... $$ to $$ ... $$
+ *  - \( ... \) and $ ... $ to $ ... $
+ */
+function preprocessLatex(content: string): string {
+  if (!content) return '';
+
+  return content
+    // Convert display brackets \[ ... \] to $$ ... $$
+    .replace(/\\\[([\s\S]*?)\\\]/g, (_, math) => `$$\n${math.trim()}\n$$`)
+    // Convert inline parentheses \( ... \) to $ ... $
+    .replace(/\\\(([\s\S]*?)\\\)/g, (_, math) => `$${math.trim()}$`)
+    // Protect raw ( W_0 \in \mathbb{R}... ) patterns emitted by some LLMs without backslashes
+    .replace(/(^|[^\\$])\(\s*([A-Za-z0-9_\\^+\-*=<>~ ]*\\(?:in|mathbb|Delta|times|mu|sigma|theta|alpha|beta|gamma|lambda|sum|prod|leq|geq|ll|gg|approx|neq|subset)[^()]*?)\s*\)/g, 
+      (match, prefix, math) => `${prefix}$${math.trim()}$`
+    );
+}

The LaTeX math equation rendering issue has been addressed and verified.

---

### Why LaTeX Was Not Rendering Previously:
1. **KaTeX Stylesheet Loading**: KaTeX requires its accompanying font assets and CSS (`katex/dist/katex.min.css`) loaded globally in the DOM. Importing it inside Tailwind's `@import "katex/dist/katex.min.css"` in Turbopack did not always bundle font faces to root layouts.
2. **LLM Output Delimiters**: LLMs frequently output math using LaTeX delimiters like `\( ... \)` and `\[ ... \]`, or raw unescaped math expressions inside plain parentheses like `( W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} )` rather than markdown's expected `$ ... $` and `$$ ... $$`.
3. **Single Dollar Configuration**: `remark-math` by default requires explicit option `{ singleDollarTextMath: true }` to interpret inline math `$ ... $`.

---

### What Was Fixed:
1. **Direct KaTeX Import**:
   - Added `import "katex/dist/katex.min.css";` directly into [`frontend_rag/app/layout.tsx`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/frontend_rag/app/layout.tsx) so all KaTeX mathematical fonts and symbol classes are available globally in the browser.
2. **Preprocessor for Formula Delimiters**:
   - Added `preprocessLatex` in [`ChatPanel.tsx`](file:///C:/document/Study%20documents/backend_rag/RAG_TS/frontend_rag/components/ChatPanel.tsx):
     - Standardizes display blocks `\[ ... \]` $\rightarrow$ `$$ ... $$`.
     - Standardizes inline equations `\( ... \)` $\rightarrow$ `$ ... $`.
     - Automatically wraps LaTeX expressions inside plain parentheses like:
       $$( W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} ) \longrightarrow \$W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\$$
       $$( W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA ) \longrightarrow \$W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA\$$
       $$( B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} ) \longrightarrow \$B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}\$$
       $$( A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} ) \longrightarrow \$A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}\$$
       $$( r \ll \min(d, k) ) \longrightarrow \$r \ll \min(d, k)\$$
3. **Remark-Math & Rehype-KaTeX Options**:
   - Configured `[remarkMath, { singleDollarTextMath: true }]`.
   - Configured `[rehypeKatex, { output: 'htmlAndMathml', throwOnError: false }]`.
4. **Build & Live Deployment**:
   - Clean production build passed (`next build`).
   - Re-launched the frontend server on port `3000` with the updated KaTeX bundle.
   - Committed across `vuong/scientific-rag-workbench` (`e7b1c68`) and root `vuong/scientific-rag-fullstack` (`420c8f3`).

Equations such as $(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k})$ and $(W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA)$ will now render cleanly in the chat interface at [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000).

2: name: design-taste-frontend
3: description: tasteskill v2, the anti-slop frontend skill. Art direction for websites, distilled from a study of 247 curated gallery sites (One Page Love, Awwwards Sites of the Day). Deals researched directions (idea, composition, type, palette, photographs, section blueprints) from a library, enforces a strict no-slop house style with a real-browser inspector, and runs a look-and-fix loop on screenshots. Use this whenever you build, design, redesign, restyle, polish or review a landing page, marketing site, portfolio, product page, one-pager, hero or any public-facing web page, in any stack (HTML/CSS, React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Astro, Tailwind) — also when the user says a page looks generic, templated, "AI-made", sloppy, or asks to make it look designed, premium, award-level or less like every other site. Not for dashboards or app screens.

5: 
6: # tasteskill v2
7: 
8: A page built by a model usually looks like the average of every page the model has seen: a centred
9: headline over three lines, a little label above it, a row of icon cards, a soft gradient, a few thin
10: rules and a monospace caption. Nothing in it is wrong and nothing in it was decided.
11: 
12: This skill replaces those defaults with decisions, in four ways:
13: 
14: 1. **A script deals the directions, you choose among them.** Asked to invent a look, a model picks
15:    the category default every time. `scripts/draw.mjs` deals three of twenty researched directions;
16:    you choose the one that carries the subject's idea, and the script then deals its type system,
17:    palette, hero and section compositions from a library distilled from 247 real sites.
18: 2. **The idea comes from the subject.** In the study, what separated the best sites from the forgettable
19:    ones was a concept taken from the thing itself, not the styling.
20: 3. **A house style with no ornaments,** measured in a real browser by `scripts/inspect.mjs`, so the
21:    rules are checked rather than hoped for.
22: 4. **You look at what you made.** Screenshots at three widths, a juror's rubric, fix, look again.
23: 
24: One warning learned in testing. Taking the ornaments away is only half the job; a page that has lost its
25: labels, rules and cards and gained nothing in their place reads as thin, and blind jurors rightly prefer
26: a richer page with tells over an empty page without them. The other half is substance: type set
27: larger, whole fields of colour, real pictures of this subject's world (found or drawn), and every
28: section carrying its full content. The skill is built to give you that; do not trade it for restraint.
29: 
30: In the commands below `<skill>` is this skill's folder. Run them from the project's root, so the
31: working files land in `.taste-skill/` there. The scripts need Node 22+ and an installed Chrome, Edge
32: or Chromium, and install nothing. `assets.mjs` also needs network access; it uses no API keys.
33: 
34: ## The run
35: 
36: Do these in order. Steps 1–5 take a few minutes and decide whether the page is any good.
37: 
38: ### 1. Read the brief and the project
39: 
40: Find out what is real: the subject, the audience, the one thing the page must get someone to do, the
41: stack, any existing brand (colours, fonts, logo), and above all **what imagery truly exists**: the
42: project's own photographs or product shots, a real interface that can be shown, an image generation
43: tool you can call, or nothing. Do not plan around pictures you do not have. Nothing of its own is
44: rarely nothing at all: the subject's city, street, materials and history are in open archives and
45: museums, free to use with a credit (step 6, `scripts/assets.mjs`).
46: 
47: If the request is vague, decide and state your reading in one line instead of asking. Ask only when a
48: missing fact blocks the work (for example, no product name).
49: 
50: Then **inventory the subject** in your notes: eight to twelve things that belong to this client and to
51: no competitor. Look for its name and what the name means; its address, door number, street and
52: neighbourhood, and what that place looks like (its tiles, signs, paint colours, typefaces on its shop
53: fronts, its light, its weather); the numbers in the brief (seats, rooms, minutes to the sea, the
54: price, the year); the constraint it lives with (only one batch a month, closed in winter, by
55: appointment); its materials and colours; its rituals and hours (the oven lit at five, the ferry at
56: seven); the printed things of its world (a timetable, a label, a ticket, a sign). This list is where
57: the idea comes from in step 4. In blind tests, the page that won each brief was built from an item on
58: such a list (the client's name and what it means, the street it stands in, the one constraint that
59: makes it what it is), and the pages that lost had a good composition with a category idea. The list
60: is also your picture search: each place, material and printed thing on it is a query for step 6.
61: 
62: ### 2. Write the argument
63: 
64: Before any design, list the page as claims with their proof, one line per section, the way
65: `references/copy.md` §1 shows. The claims decide which sections exist and in what order. Delete any
66: section that has no claim. This is how you avoid the stock sequence of hero, logos, three features,
67: testimonial, pricing, call to action.
68: 
69: ### 3. Draw the direction
70: 
71: ```bash
72: node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --sector <sector> --brief "<one line about the subject>" \
73:   --sections <roles in the order of your argument> [--tone <tone>] [--have <assets>] [--keep palette,type] \
74:   --options 3
75: ```
76: 
77: This deals three directions and prints a short summary of each. Hold each one against your inventory:
78: which way of composing can carry something only this client has? Choose that one, not the most
79: familiar, and write one line in your notes on why. In testing, a single random direction that did not
80: suit the subject was the commonest cause of a weak page. Then deal the full sheet:
81: 
82: ```bash
83: node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs <the same arguments, without --options> --direction <chosen id>
84: ```
85: 
86: - `--sector`: `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --list sectors`. Pick the closest.
87: - `--sections`: roles from `--list roles` (features, showcase, how-it-works, testimonial, proof, stats,
88:   pricing, faq, cta, footer, intro, about, work, gallery, list, contact). The hero is implied.
89: - `--tone` (optional): quiet, bold, warm, technical, playful, luxury, editorial. Only pass it when the
90:   brief clearly asks for one.
91: - `--have`: assets that really exist, comma-separated: `photography` (the project's own photographs of
92:   the place, people or work), `product-photo` (photographs of the specific product, or an image tool
93:   that can make them), `product-ui` (real screenshots), `illustration`, `video`. Leave it out if you
94:   have none: the draw then avoids compositions that depend on them and the sheet says how to fill
95:   picture slots honestly (software shows its own interface built in HTML; a product with no photographs
96:   is drawn and set among real pictures of its world, never a fake product shot). Pictures you will
97:   find in the open collections are not the project's own; leave them out of `--have`.
98: - `--keep palette,type`: when the brand already fixes colours or typefaces. The draw then deals only
99:   the composition, and you map the brand's values onto the roles.
100: 
101: The command prints a **direction sheet**. It is the art direction for this build:
102: 
103: - **Adopt it.** Do not blend it with the layout you would have made anyway. If it feels unfamiliar,
104:   good: the familiar layout is the one this skill exists to prevent.
105: - Redraw one slot (`--redraw hero | type | palette | photos | section:<role> | direction`) only for a
106:   reason you can state: it contradicts a stated brand constraint, or needs an asset that does not
107:   exist. Never redraw to get something more comfortable. Record every redraw in your report.
108: - When a dealt section cannot hold the real content (it compares three plans and there is one price;
109:   it wants five quotations and there are none), do not bend the content to fit. List the others with
110:   `--alternatives <role>`, pick the one whose assumptions match the content, and take it with
111:   `--redraw section:<role>=<id>`.
112: - **Check the palette against the subject.** A dealt palette is a set of proportions (one ground, one
113:   ink, one accent, fields) as much as a set of colours. If its colours fight the subject's own material
114:   (candy pastels for a peat whisky, neon for a mountain hut), redraw the palette once; if the subject
115:   has unmistakable colours of its own (its material, the paint of its street, the landscape outside
116:   its windows), keep the dealt proportions and take the colours from the subject instead, and say so
117:   in the report.
118: - Reprint it any time with `node <skill>/scripts/draw.mjs --show`. In a long session, re-read it before each
119:   section you build.
120: 
121: ### 4. Find the idea
122: 
123: The direction is a way of composing. The idea is what makes the page belong to this subject and no
124: other. Write this sentence in your notes and do not start building until both blanks are filled from
125: the subject itself:
126: 
127: > On this page, **[something that belongs to the subject]** becomes **[the device the direction calls for]**.
128: 
129: Places to look for the first blank:
130: 
131: - **Its output.** What does the thing produce? Put the real output on the page as material. (A camera
132:   that prints poems delivered its copy as paper slips.)
133: - **Its object or shape.** What does it physically look like, in cross-section, in silhouette?
134:   Enlarge it, crop it, make it the frame or the one motif.
135: - **Its name.** Can the letters hold a photograph, stack into a wall, split to two corners?
136: - **Its place.** Is there one view that makes someone want to be there?
137: - **Its ritual.** Is there a sequence the page can perform as it scrolls?
138: - **Its artefact.** What printed thing already exists in its world: ticket, menu, label, receipt,
139:   invitation, folder, manual?
140: - **Its opposite.** Which other category owns the feeling this one lacks?
141: 
142: Fill the first blank from your inventory (step 1), not from the category. **The competitor test:** put
143: the nearest real competitor in the sentence (the bakery two streets away, another oak furniture maker,
144: another hut on the same mountain). If the sentence still works, the idea belongs to the category: a
145: loaf of bread is every bakery; the seven doors of the street this one is named after are only this one.
146: "Clean and modern" is not an idea. The sites the study's panel scored lowest were the ones whose idea
147: was recorded as "none beyond the standard formula".
148: 
149: **One live thing.** Give the page one thing the visitor can do, or that is different for each visit,
150: made from the idea: pick a wood and see the chair in it; type your name and see it cut in the
151: foundry's letters; set the loan and read the real monthly figure; see whether the hut's stove is lit
152: right now and how long until the last ferry; choose a size and see it against the room. In blind tests every winning page had one and the jurors named it first. Rules: it uses the subject's real content, it works on a phone with a thumb, it has a plain
153: fallback without script, it never blocks reading, and it is one thing, not a playground. It is
154: built in step 6 as part of the page, not added as motion in step 9.
155: 
156: ### 5. Write the words
157: 
158: Write the whole page as a copy deck (plain text) before markup, following `references/copy.md`:
159: 
160: - **Every headline fits in two lines or fewer at every width.** Do the arithmetic in copy.md §2 before
161:   committing to a sentence: about 32 characters is safe everywhere at a confident size. The studied
162:   gallery heroes have a median of 5 words and 32 characters.
163: - One supporting sentence. One primary action, named for what it does, as a real button on the first
164:   screen.
165: - **The first screen answers the visitor's first question in large type.** For an event: what it is,
166:   when and where (the dates belong in the headline or at the second size, never only in small text).
167:   For a product: what it is and what it costs or does. For a person: who and what they do. Every
168:   section the visitor came for (the line-up, the menu, the rooms, the price) has its own heading and
169:   its own place in the navigation.
170: - **Write the full content.** Every section the brief asks for delivers its information completely:
171:   the whole menu with prices, each room with its own details, every speaker and talk, the price with
172:   what it includes, an answer for each real question. Thin sections are the commonest reason a clean
173:   page loses to a busier one.
174: - Sample details are expected where the brief leaves gaps (dish names, room names and rates, project
175:   titles) so the design is seen at full density; list them in the report for the client to confirm.
176:   Proof is never invented: no customers, quotes, reviews, press, logos or business statistics.
177: 
178: ### 6. Build it, still
179: 
180: Build the page with motion switched off in your head; a page that needs animation to look finished is
181: not finished. Order of work:
182: 
183: 1. **Tokens.** Colour and type roles from the sheet as CSS custom properties. Everything downstream
184:    references tokens only. `<skill>/assets/base.css` is a neutral foundation you may start from (reset, token
185:    names, fluid type steps, grid, focus and selection styles, the motion helpers); it has no look of
186:    its own.
187: 2. **The hero, exactly as the blueprint describes it,** at desktop and at phone width. Get the big
188:    thing big and the small things small before anything else exists.
189: 3. **Each section from its blueprint,** with this project's content. Keep the geometry, change the
190:    subject. Neighbouring sections must not share a layout. **Carry the idea into every section,**
191:    pricing, FAQ and footer included: the commonest failure in the study, even among good sites, is a
192:    distinctive first screen followed by stock blocks.
193: 4. **Imagery,** in this order of preference:
194:    1. the project's own;
195:    2. generated, if you have an image tool;
196:    3. **real pictures of the subject's world from the open collections,** whenever an honest one
197:       exists. Search them with `node <skill>/scripts/assets.mjs "<query>"` (Openverse, Wikimedia
198:       Commons, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Met; only licences that allow commercial use, by
199:       default). Search the inventory, not the category: its street in old postcards, an old map of the
200:       neighbourhood, its material up close, its trade in engravings, a museum object of its kind, a
201:       botanical plate, a star chart. Use them large and with intent: one archival photograph as the
202:       hero, an engraving enlarged into the page's motif, the real map of the street as the contact
203:       section. Look at each before choosing; `--get <ref>` downloads it into `assets/` and records
204:       its source and licence, and `--credits` prints the credit line for the footer. A found picture
205:       shows the world around the client and is never presented as the client's own product, room,
206:       dish, person or team;
207:    4. **drawn in code from the subject itself,** for what no honest picture exists of (its objects,
208:       its tiles, its windows, its product's interface, made as one consistent flat graphic language in
209:       the palette's real colours);
210:    5. the photographs dealt on the sheet, only where an honestly generic picture fits (the sea for a
211:       sea house), never as a stand-in for the subject;
212:    6. type and colour alone.
213: 
214:    **The floor, which the inspector checks:** at least four real pictures on the page, usually six to
215:    twelve (photographs, archival images, maps, engravings, footage, raster artwork; for software, its
216:    cropped interface fragments count too). SVG drawings do not count toward the floor: draw what no
217:    picture exists of, and still carry real pictures. Add one moving picture wherever an honest clip
218:    exists: search it with `assets.mjs --video "<query>"` and use it as a muted loop with a poster
219:    frame. Models skip pictures and footage because finding them is work; the page fails without them.
220: 
221:    `references/imagery.md` covers searching, licences and credits, video, drawing, crops and treatments.
222: 5. **The live thing** from step 4, built into the section where it proves the claim (often the hero
223:    or the booking), with real content, a thumb-sized phone version and a plain fallback.
224: 6. **Fullness.** Look at each desktop screen as a poster: one dominant thing and the content it
225:    carries. A screen that is mostly empty ground is an underbuilt section, not a rest; one deliberate
226:    rest per page is the limit, and the inspector fails a page with two or more near-empty screens.
227:    Running text is in the full ink at 16px or more; grey is for secondary notes.
228: 7. **States and semantics.** Real links and buttons, visible focus, alt text, a phone layout that is
229:    its own composition.
230: 
231: Read `references/type.md`, `references/colour.md` and `references/layout.md` when you need the detail
232: behind a decision; the laws below are the short form.
233: 
234: ### 7. Gate
235: 
236: ```bash
237: node <skill>/scripts/lint.mjs <source files or folder>
238: node <skill>/scripts/inspect.mjs <url or path/to/index.html>
239: ```
240: 
241: `lint.mjs` scans source for banned patterns and stock phrases. `inspect.mjs` opens the page in a real
242: browser at 1440, 768 and 390 pixels, measures it (headline line counts, type sizes, fonts actually
243: loaded, colours, rules, shadows, gradients, contrast, overflow) and saves screenshots to
244: `.taste-skill/inspect/`. Fix every `FAIL`. Treat each `WARN` as wrong unless you can defend it to a
245: designer in one sentence. Re-run until there are no `FAIL`s. Do not argue with the meter and do not
246: hide things from it. The inspector serves local files over a throwaway local server; if the page must
247: also open straight from the file system, open `index.html` that way once before you finish.
248: 
249: ### 8. Look
250: 
251: Passing the gate means nothing banned was measured. It does not mean the page is good. Open the
252: screenshots the inspector lists (every viewport, with your image viewer or Read tool) and critique them
253: with `references/critique.md`: the fourteen passes, the Awwwards-weighted score, the caps. Write the critique
254: down in its format, fix the top three problems, run the inspector again, look again. Three rounds at
255: most.
256: 
257: Judge only the pictures. If a problem is visible in a screenshot, it is real, whatever the code says.
258: 
259: ### 9. Move
260: 
261: Now build the motion layer. It is required, and it is more than one fade: the inspector counts the
262: elements that really move while the page loads and is scrolled, and fails a page under eight (it warns
263: under sixteen). The layer has four parts:
264: 
265: 1. **The signature move** named on the sheet: one, done well.
266: 2. **An entrance for the parts of every section:** the heading, then the text, then the picture,
267:    staggered by 60–90ms, rising 16–32px with opacity, triggered once as the section enters. Not one
268:    fade for the whole block, and never content that stays hidden if the script fails.
269: 3. **Feedback on every control:** press, hover and focus on buttons, links, cards and the live thing.
270: 4. **One moving picture:** a found clip as a muted loop, a slow scale or drift on a photograph, or a
271:    scroll-linked move on the hero picture.
272: 
273: Transform and opacity only; every move has a `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback that keeps the content
274: and drops the travel. A move that changes the colour or the layout of whole screens (colour by
275: chapter, a pinned story) is part of the composition, so build it in step 6 and let every look round see
276: it. `references/motion.md` has the tokens and tested recipes. Then run the inspector once more and check
277: every screenshot for content that failed to appear.
278: 
279: ### 10. Report
280: 
281: Tell the user, briefly: the direction dealt (name and seed) and any redraws with reasons; the idea
282: sentence and the live thing; the final scores from your last critique round and what still falls short;
283: every found picture and clip with its title, creator, licence and source page (`assets.mjs --credits` prints
284: the list) and where its credit sits on the page; which bundled photographs and which drawings stand in
285: for photography (so they can be replaced); and any sample content that must be swapped before launch.
286: Do not claim a check you did not run.
287: 
288: ## House rules
289: 
290: These hold on every build, whatever the direction. `inspect.mjs` measures them.
291: 
292: | Rule | Instead |
293: | --- | --- |
294: | **Headlines: two lines or fewer, at every width.** Every `h1`–`h6`, and the main line of the first screen whatever its tag. | Cut words. Then widen the measure. Size last. |
295: | **Statements are paragraphs.** An intro sentence or a quotation set large is marked up as `<p>` or `<blockquote>`, stays at statement size (36px or less on desktop, 24px on a phone) and runs to about 25 words, three lines. | Larger than that it is a headline and the two-line rule applies. In blind tests jurors read a 42px sentence over four lines as a four-line headline. |
296: | **No eyebrows.** No small label above a heading, no pill badge above the headline, no "New ·" chip. | Put the information in the heading or the first sentence, or drop it. |
297: | **No monospace** outside real code blocks. | The text face. Tabular figures where numbers align. |
298: | **No index numbering.** No 01 / 02 / 03, no (001), no "Step 2". | Order shown by position, size, or the words. A real `<ol>` if order matters. |
299: | **No thin rules.** No hairline dividers, no 1px outlined boxes, no grid lines, crosshairs or crop marks. | Space. A step in background tone. A change of scale. A filled shape. |
300: | **No gradients.** Not as backgrounds, not on buttons, not in text. | Flat colour, or a real photograph. A neutral scrim under text on a photo is the one exception. |
301: | **No shadows on things at rest.** No glows. | A tone step between surfaces. Shadows only on what truly floats: a menu, a dialog. |
302: | **No assistant palette.** No yellow-cream ground with terracotta or rust; no violet or indigo. | The dealt palette. |
303: | **No tiny uppercase letter-spaced labels.** | Sentence case at a readable size. |
304: | **No icon-topped feature cards, no rows of identical cards.** | The dealt section blueprint. |
305: | **No glass.** No backdrop blur panels, no floating pill navigation. | A plain bar: wordmark, a few links, one action. |
306: | **No emoji, no gradient blobs, no decorative shapes, no fake dashboards of grey bars.** | A real picture, a real interface fragment, or nothing. |
307: | **No styled accent word** in a headline (italic, serif, coloured, underlined). | One face, one colour. The words carry the emphasis. |
308: | **Two typefaces at most,** usually one. | The dealt type system. |
309: 
310: Three places keep their own conventions and are left alone by the inspector: real code in
311: `<pre>`/`<code>` (monospace is correct there), real tables and form fields (they may have lines), and
312: a real interface fragment whose root carries the attribute `data-ui` (the product's own borders and
313: menus; see `references/imagery.md` §7).
314: 
315: Why these, honestly. Some are what the study measured: among the 247 sites, those the panel scored
316: 7.5 or higher used icon feature cards 1% of the time against 28% for sites under 6.5, pill badges 14%
317: against 34%, gradients 22% against 52%, shadows 24% against 48%, tiny tracked caps 16% against 57%.
318: Others are the owner's taste and go against current gallery fashion: monospace labels, index numbers
319: and hairline grids are actually *more* common on award sites than on weak ones, which is exactly why
320: generators imitate them and why they now read as costume. They are banned here without exception.
321: `references/tells.md` keeps the dated registry.
322: 
323: Removing ornament leaves space. Never fill it with another ornament. Fill it with scale (make the main
324: thing larger), with the full content, with a picture made for this subject, or with a field of flat
325: colour. Leave it empty on purpose once per page at most.

327: ## Laws of the craft
328: 
329: Short form. Numbers are from the study unless marked as house style.
330: 
331: **Type**
332: - Two or three sizes do the visible work: one very large, one small, nothing in between. Median
333:   headline-to-body ratio on the studied sites is 4.3; the best go far beyond (largest type: median
334:   8.4vw on the top sites against 5.0vw on the weak ones).
335: - Display type: tracking -0.02 to -0.05em, leading 0.85–1.05. Text: 16–20px, leading 1.45–1.6,
336:   45–75 characters per line.
337: - Five sizes on a page is the ceiling. One family is normal (a third of the studied sites); two is the
338:   limit.
339: - Left-aligned by default. Centre at most one moment.
340: 
341: **Space**
342: - One grid, one pair of tight margins (16–32px), used everywhere; large things run to the edges. Text
343:   blocks share two or three left edges on the whole page.
344: - The gap between sections is clearly larger than any gap inside one: 120–220px on desktop.
345: - Each section has a different composition from its neighbours; none is a card grid.
346: 
347: **Colour**
348: - One ground, one ink, one accent. The accent appears on the action and perhaps one other thing.
349: - Running text in the full ink. A page set in soft grey reads unfinished.
350: - Surfaces are separated by a small step in tone, never by a line or a shadow.
351: - A section may change the whole field colour. Nothing fades into anything.
352: 
353: **Imagery**
354: - One dominant image beats six small ones. On the top-scored sites the hero media covers at least half
355:   the first screen 68% of the time.
356: - Same crop ratios, same treatment, square corners unless the direction says otherwise (73% of the
357:   studied sites leave media square).
358: - No image is better than a placeholder, an icon, or an abstract shape. A picture drawn for this
359:   subject, in its colours and with care, is better than either. A real picture of its world, found
360:   and credited, is better still.
361: - Every found picture is downloaded into the project, credited on the page and listed in the report.
362:   None is presented as the client's own.
363: - Nothing ever lies on top of a headline or a statement (the inspector fails it).
364: 
365: **Components**
366: - Buttons: flat, one fill colour, either square-cornered or fully round, decided once (top sites: 52%
367:   square, 23% pill; the 9–16px "soft" radius is the weak-site default). Most strong heroes have no
368:   button at all, or one.
369: - Navigation: wordmark, three to five plain links, one action. No bar chrome.
370: - The footer is a designed close, not a sitemap: on most strong sites the name returns at full width.
371: 
372: ## Special cases
373: 
374: **An existing brand or design system.** Pass `--keep palette,type`, map the brand's colours and faces
375: onto the roles, and take only composition from the draw. The house rules still apply; if the brand
376: itself requires a banned device (its logo sits in a gradient, its accent is violet), keep the brand
377: asset, say so in the report, and pass `--allow <rule>` to the inspector for that rule only.
378: 
379: **Redesign or review of an existing page.** Run `lint.mjs` and `inspect.mjs` on it first and report
380: what they find, then critique the screenshots with `references/critique.md`. For a redesign, draw a
381: direction and proceed from step 2, keeping the page's real content and working behaviour.
382: 
383: **A component or a single section, not a page.** Skip the draw unless there is no direction to follow.
384: Match the surrounding design, apply the house rules and the laws, and still inspect the result.
385: 
386: **No checkout, no form backend.** The primary button goes to the real destination when the brief names
387: one. Otherwise it opens an email with a written subject and body (`mailto:` with the visitor's choices
388: filled in), or, for a shop, it points at `#checkout` and the report says it must be wired before
389: launch. Never fake a payment form.

409: | `references/research.md` | The study: method, numbers, what the best and worst sites do. Cite it, do not guess. |
410: | `scripts/draw.mjs` | Deals and reprints the direction; `--photos`, `--site <id>` for more references. |

1: # Colour
2: 
3: The direction sheet deals a palette with named roles. This file is how to apply it so the page looks
4: decided rather than tinted.
5: 
6: ## Contents
7: 
8: 1. What the study measured
9: 2. The roles
10: 3. Proportion
11: 4. Surfaces without lines or shadows
12: 5. Colour fields
13: 6. Dark pages
14: 7. Colour and photographs
15: 8. Contrast
16: 9. Banned families, and what "warm" means here
17: 
18: ## 1. What the study measured
19: 
20: - 41% of the studied pages are dark, 59% light. A quarter sit on pure white; 12% on pure black.
21: - Schemes, as the panel classed them: monochrome plus one accent 23%, light neutral 22%, dark neutral
22:   14%, several flat colours 13%, strictly two-tone 12%, colour carried by photographs 9%, one saturated
23:   field 6%.
24: - Buttons are neutral (black, white, grey) on 52% of sites. A coloured button is a choice, not a
25:   requirement.
26: - Gradient fills appear on 22% of the top-scored sites and 52% of the weak ones; gradient text on 2%
27:   against 13%.
28: - One site in 246 has a terracotta primary button and none has a violet one. Those are colours of
29:   generated pages, not of the gallery. Warm off-white grounds do occur (32 sites), nearly always with
30:   a dark or green ink rather than an orange accent.
31: - Top-scored sites change the page's field colour between sections more often (a median of two section
32:   grounds against one).
33: 
34: ## 2. The roles
35: 
36: ```css
37: :root {
38:   --bg: …;          /* the ground: most of the surface */
39:   --surface: …;     /* one tone step from the ground: filled panels, form fields, tiles */
40:   --ink: …;         /* main text and the strongest marks */
41:   --muted: …;       /* secondary text; still passes contrast on --bg */
42:   --accent: …;      /* the one accent */
43:   --accent-ink: …;  /* text on the accent */
44:   /* --field-1 … --field-n and their inks, when the palette has section fields */
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: Use the tokens for every colour in the build. A raw hex in a component is a second palette starting.
49: Do not add greys between the roles: if you need a quieter text, it is `--muted`; if you need a quieter
50: surface, it is `--surface`.
51: 
52: ## 3. Proportion
53: 
54: Decide the shares before colouring anything and check them in the screenshot:
55: 
56: - **Ground:** 70–90% of the page.
57: - **Ink:** text and perhaps one inverted section (ink as ground, ground as ink).
58: - **Accent:** under 5% of any screen. It marks the action and at most one other recurring thing. The
59:   moment it appears in five places it stops meaning "here".
60: 
61: Palettes with fields (flat-loud, pastel) work differently: each section is one field at full strength
62: and the proportion rule applies inside each section (field, its ink, nothing else).
63: 
64: The accent is not for headings, icons, bullets, borders or underlines unless the direction sheet says
65: so. A headline is ink.
66: 
67: ## 4. Surfaces without lines or shadows
68: 
69: With rules and shadows banned, a surface is told apart from the ground by tone alone:
70: 
71: ```css
72: .panel { background: var(--surface); }          /* 2–6 lightness points from --bg */
73: .field { background: var(--surface); border: 0; } /* inputs: filled, with a clear focus state */
74: .field:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }
75: ```
76: 
77: - One step is enough. If a panel does not read, increase padding or separate with space before
78:   reaching for a second tone.
79: - Do not nest a panel inside a panel.
80: - Images do not need a frame. If a light photograph melts into a light ground, change the crop or set
81:   it on `--surface`, do not outline it.
82: - A thick bar (4px or more) in ink or accent is a graphic element, allowed where the direction uses
83:   it. A 1px line is not.
84: 
85: ## 5. Colour fields
86: 
87: A section that changes the whole ground colour is the strongest colour move available, and it replaces
88: dividers, cards and background decoration at once.
89: 
90: - Fields meet edge to edge with a hard line. Nothing fades.
91: - Every field has its own assigned ink from the palette. Never put `--muted` on a coloured field; use
92:   the field's ink at full strength, or at 70% opacity for secondary text if it still passes contrast.
93: - Neighbouring fields should differ in lightness, not only in hue, or the page vibrates.
94: - Order them like chapters: open strong, rest, surprise, close dark or very light.
95: - The page's meta theme colour and the navigation follow the first field.
96: 
97: ## 6. Dark pages
98: 
99: - Put `color-scheme: dark` on the root so form controls and scrollbars follow.
100: - The ground is a deep tone with a slight tint from the palette, and the ink is a soft light, not
101:   `#fff` on `#000`, unless the palette deals exactly that for a stark two-tone direction.
102: - Secondary text is where dark pages fail: check `--muted` against the ground (4.5:1).
103: - Depth on dark comes from a lighter surface step, never from glows or coloured light.
104: - Use lighter font weights than you would on a light page.
105: 
106: ## 7. Colour and photographs
107: 
108: - When photographs carry the colour, the interface stays neutral and takes its ink from the darkest
109:   tone in the imagery.
110: - Do not wash a photograph with the brand colour. Either leave it alone, or commit to a real treatment
111:   for every image on the page (all greyscale, or all untouched).
112: - Text over a photograph needs a calm region. If there is none, move the text off the image. A neutral
113:   scrim (black or the ink colour, 30–55% opacity, flat or fading over the text area only) is the one
114:   gradient the inspector allows.
115: - A flat field sampled from a photograph (its sky, its shadow) makes a section sit with that image.
116: 
117: ## 8. Contrast
118: 
119: - Body text 4.5:1 or better; display type and large numerals 3:1 or better; the dealt palettes meet
120:   7:1 for ink on ground.
121: - `inspect.mjs` computes contrast for text on flat grounds and fails anything under 2.6:1. It cannot
122:   see text over photographs: check those in the screenshots yourself.
123: - Do not lower opacity on text to make it "soft" unless you have checked the resulting ratio.
124: - Focus states and hover states increase contrast, never reduce it.
125: 
126: ## 9. Banned families, and what "warm" means here
127: 
128: The inspector fails these:
129: 
130: - **Cream with terracotta.** A yellow-cream ground (roughly hue 22–62, light and noticeably
131:   saturated) with a rust, clay or burnt-orange accent is the house look of AI assistants and of the
132:   pages they generate. Either half alone is suspect; together they are unmistakable.
133: - **Violet and indigo.** The first wave of generated pages was purple; it still reads that way.
134: 
135: If the brief wants warmth, get it from a low-chroma stone, bone or putty ground (saturation under
136: about 15%), from a deep green, brown or oxblood ink, from photographs, or from a full warm field
137: (mustard, tomato red, pink) used flat and with conviction. Warmth is not beige.
138: 
139: If the brand itself owns one of the banned colours, it is the brand's and you keep it: use
140: `--keep palette`, pass `--allow palette-purple` (or the relevant rule) to the inspector, and note it in
141: the report.
142:

1: # Tells — the dated registry
2: 
3: A tell is a device that makes a page read as generated. Tells are not bad design in themselves; most
4: began as good ideas on good sites. They became tells by being produced by default, everywhere, without
5: a reason. That is why this registry is dated, and why it never names a replacement font, colour or
6: component: every published "use this instead" list has become the next wave of tells within months.
7: Replacements here are procedures (draw from the library, derive from the subject), not products.
8: 
9: `scripts/inspect.mjs` and `scripts/lint.mjs` detect most entries. Status: **banned** means the
10: inspector fails the page; **warned** means it flags it and you need a reason.
11: 
12: ## Contents
13: 
14: 1. First wave (2023–2024)
15: 2. Second wave (2025)
16: 3. Third wave (2025–2026): the "fix" that became the look
17: 4. Gallery fashion, banned as house style
18: 5. Structural tells
19: 6. Copy tells
20: 7. Motion tells
21: 8. Why removal is not enough
22: 
23: ## 1. First wave (2023–2024)
24: 
25: | Tell | Status | Do instead |
26: | --- | --- | --- |
27: | Violet / indigo gradients on hero, buttons and glows | banned | The dealt palette; flat colour |
28: | Gradient-filled headline text | banned | Solid ink |
29: | Glass panels: backdrop blur, translucent cards | warned (2 or more) | Opaque surfaces one tone step from the ground |
30: | Glowing or gradient "Get started" button | banned | Flat button named for its action |
31: | Soft grey drop shadow under every card | banned | Tone step, or no box |
32: | Three identical feature cards, each with an icon in a rounded square | banned | The dealt section blueprint |
33: | Emoji as icons or bullets | banned | Words, or a real picture |
34: | Centred headline, subtitle, two buttons, screenshot below | no rule; the draw avoids it | The dealt hero |
35: | The same typeface on every generated page | warned (lint: default-font) | The dealt type system |
36: 
37: ## 2. Second wave (2025)
38: 
39: | Tell | Status | Do instead |
40: | --- | --- | --- |
41: | Eyebrow / kicker: tiny tracked uppercase label above every heading | banned | Fold it into the heading, or delete |
42: | Pill badge above the hero headline ("New", "Beta", "Introducing") | banned | Say it in the supporting sentence |
43: | One word of the headline in italic serif, colour or underline | warned | One face, one colour |
44: | Bento grid of rounded tiles as the feature section | warned as card rows | A composed section; tiles only in the dense-tiles direction, filled, strict sizes |
45: | Near-black ground with one neon accent and a glow | banned via shadow, gradient | A dealt dark palette, no glow |
46: | Floating rounded pill navigation with blur | warned | A plain bar |
47: | Fake dashboard hero built from grey bars and donut charts | no rule; see imagery.md §7 | A real interface fragment, or no image |
48: | Decorative status dot ("Available for work", pulsing "live") | lint: bounce | Remove |
49: | Fade-and-rise on every section | no rule; see motion.md | One signature move |
50: 
51: ## 3. Third wave (2025–2026): the "fix" that became the look
52: 
53: The remedy published for the first two waves was "warm it up and make it editorial". Models adopted
54: the remedy wholesale and it is now the most recognisable generated look of all.
55: 
56: | Tell | Status | Do instead |
57: | --- | --- | --- |
58: | Yellow-cream ground + terracotta / rust / clay accent | banned together; terracotta banned alone; cream warned | The dealt palette. Warmth from a low-chroma stone, a deep ink, a photograph, or a full warm field |
59: | High-contrast or soft serif display as the shortcut to "premium" | no rule | The dealt type system, whatever class it is |
60: | Oversized italic serif headline | no rule | As dealt |
61: | Broadsheet cosplay: hairline rules everywhere, zero radius, dense columns | banned via hairline | Structure from space and tone |
62: | "Field notes", "Quietly trusted by", "On our desks": performative labels | lint: copy | Plain section names |
63: 
64: ## 4. Gallery fashion, banned as house style
65: 
66: These are common on award sites right now. In the study they appear *more* often on the top-scored
67: sites than on the weak ones (panel observations: monospace labels 44% against 24%, index numbering 38%
68: against 21%; measured thin rules 61% against 52%). They are banned here regardless, by the owner's
69: decision: they are the first things a generator copies from the gallery, they carry no information,
70: and a page built without them has to find real structure.
71: 
72: | Tell | Status | Do instead |
73: | --- | --- | --- |
74: | Monospace micro-labels, mono as a "technical" voice, mono captions | banned | The text face; tabular figures for data |
75: | Index numbering: 01 / 02 / 03, (001), "Step 02", numbered section markers | banned | Order by position, scale, or the words; `<ol>` when it is truly a list |
76: | Thin rules: hairline dividers, ruled grids, 1px outlined boxes and tiles | banned (boxes: 3 or more) | Space, tone steps, filled shapes, a thick bar if a bar is the idea |
77: | Design-tool chrome as ornament: crosshairs, crop marks, selection handles, dashed guides, rulers | banned via hairline, dashed | Remove |
78: | Agency micro-meta: local time, coordinates, weather, version stamps, "©2026 — Scroll", middle-dot strings | lint: copy; micro-label | Remove |
79: | Tiny uppercase letter-spaced captions scattered around the viewport | banned (3 or more) | Sentence case at readable size, placed with the content it describes |
80: 
81: Tiny tracked capitals are the one item in this group the data condemns as well: 16% of top sites
82: against 57% of weak ones.
83: 
84: ## 5. Structural tells
85: 
86: | Tell | Status | Do instead |
87: | --- | --- | --- |
88: | Headline as a full sentence at display size, three or four lines | banned (over two lines) | A title of about five words; the rest goes below |
89: | Stock section order: hero, logos, features, testimonial, pricing, CTA | no rule; see copy.md §1 | The order of the argument |
90: | Every section the same layout family | critique.md pass 9 | Different composition per section, from the sheet |
91: | Everything centred | warned over 72% | Left-anchored, one centred moment |
92: | One medium border radius (12–16px) on everything | none | Square or fully round, chosen once |
93: | Nine nearly equal font sizes | warned over 9 | Five sizes, far apart |
94: | Invented social proof: logos, quotes, star rows, "10,000+ teams" | copy.md §5 | Real proof, or none |
95: | Text or a CSS box where a picture belongs | critique.md cap | A real picture, or a design that needs none |
96: 
97: ## 6. Copy tells
98: 
99: Flagged by `lint.mjs`: the genre's verbs and adjectives (unlock, supercharge, seamless, elevate,
100: effortless, cutting-edge, all-in-one …); the correction ("not just X, it's Y"); tricolon headlines;
101: "Get started" and "Learn more" as labels; more than a handful of em dashes; lorem ipsum. See
102: `copy.md` §6.
103: 
104: ## 7. Motion tells
105: 
106: Identical fade-up on every block; a dozen staggered hero entrances; hover lift on every card; bounce
107: easing; infinite loops that mean nothing; reveals that fail and leave a blank band. See `motion.md` §7.
108: 
109: ## 8. Why removal is not enough
110: 
111: A page with every tell removed and nothing put in their place is an empty page with good manners, and
112: that is a tell too (the "avoidance aesthetic": anyone could guess it from the category plus the list of
113: things to avoid). The tells were filling a gap where an idea should have been. The order of work in
114: `SKILL.md` exists to fill that gap first: the idea from the subject, the dealt composition, real
115: pictures or committed type, and only then the checks.
116:

# 3 directions dealt for this brief

Choose the one whose way of composing can best carry an idea from your inventory (SKILL.md steps 1 and 4), not the
most familiar one. Then deal it in full with the same command plus `--direction <id>` (and without --options).

## `colour-chapters` — Colour chapters
Idea engine: Every section is a chapter with its own flat colour, floor to ceiling. The page reads like a set of posters hung in a row, held together by one typeface and one grid.
Composition: Sections are full-bleed fields, each at least 90svh tall, butted directly against each other with no gap and no divider. Inside every field the same 12-column grid and the same margins apply, and each field holds one thing: a huge heading (8–12vw) with a small paragraph, or one photograph with a caption, or one list.

## `sentence-as-layout` — The sentence is the layout
Idea engine: One short sentence, set at poster scale, is the composition. The trick that makes it an idea rather than a big headline: something from the subject sits inside the sentence where a word would be.
Composition: The sentence is four to seven words and runs as one or two full-width lines at 9–13vw. Inline with the type, on the baseline, sits one media slot: a rounded-rectangle or square frame exactly one line-height tall and two to three ems wide, holding a photograph or a looping crop.

## `editorial-report` — The printed annual
Idea engine: Lay the page out like a well-designed printed report or magazine feature: a masthead image, a tight oversized title, text held to a strict column line, and colour used in solid blocks the way a two-colour print job would. It gives weight and authority to subjects that are really about content: findings, a manifesto, a programme, a serious product.
Composition: A fixed vertical axis at about 42% of the viewport width organises everything: headings begin on it, body columns hang from it, and the 0–42% zone holds small side notes, figures or stays empty. Masthead: a wide image band (photographic mosaic or a single crop) across the top 45% of the first screen; below it the title at 7–9vw starting on the axis, with a two-sentence standfirst at 20–24px.
